t: the positive commandment to rest in the Sabbatical year etc.. Regarding the obligation of this mitzvah in our times see below 10:9.
from working the land. Actions done to the ground.
and working the trees. Actions done to the trees themselves.
he does not receive Torah lashes etc.. For only these four kinds of work are explicit in the verse (Leviticus 25:4-5).
sowing. Which is working the land.
pruning. Zemirah, cutting the branches of the tree to improve it, which is work on the tree.

reaping. Reaping for the sake of working the land (so that more grain will grow; see Hilchot Shabbat 8:4). And below, 4:1, a different prohibition will be discussed, of reaping the crop when done in the usual way (Yad Peshutah).

harvesting. Harvesting grapes for the sake of working the tree (to improve the rest of the fruit). And below, 4:22, a different prohibition will be discussed, of harvesting fruit when done in the usual way (Yad Peshutah).
and the same applies to the vineyard and to other trees. Their law is the same.
and pruning is included in sowing. Since the purpose of pruning is to make fruit grow.
along with the other principal categories not specified in this matter. Such as plowing, which is a principal category of labor regarding Shabbat (Hilchot Shabbat 7:2).
rabbinic lashes for rebelliousness. Lashes by Rabbinic law.

one who plows or digs. Plowing with a plow drawn by an animal, and digging with a digging tool (Pe'at HaShulchan 20:2); some explain that plowing is of the entire field or a plot, while digging is in a single spot (Derekh Emunah).
one who clears stones. Removes stones from the field.
one who fertilizes. Spreads manure to enrich the soil.
one who layers. Bends a branch attached to a tree and buries it in the ground so that another tree will grow from it.
one who grafts. Inserts a detached branch into another tree so that it will fuse with it and grow.
the blemishes. Defects that develop in the tree.
and he may not strip off dry leaves and branches. He may not remove dry leaves or branches from the tree.
and he may not dust its foliage with dust. He may not scatter dust on it for the tree's benefit (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevi'it 2:2).
and he may not smoke it. He may not produce smoke.
with something that has a foul odor. A foul smell that drives away animals.
and he may not smear the unripe figs or pierce them. In order to hasten their ripening.
and he may not bind the saplings. He may not tie their branches upward (ibid. 2:4).
and he may not trim them. He may not cut off the tops of the branches, and likewise he may not scatter ash for the tree's benefit (ibid.).
and he may not cut back. "Yefasseg" is like "yefassek" (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Parah 11:9): he may not cut from the trees for the sake of renewed growth.
a thicket of reeds. A tangle of reed plants.
because it is working the ground. For he burns them to prepare the ground for sowing.
and one does not train a cow to plow except on sand. When training it for plowing, one does so in a place not fit for sowing, where he does not look like he is plowing.
and one does not test seeds. To see whether they are good.
in a pot full of earth. Since sometimes one sows in a pot, and he would look like he is sowing.
but one may test them in a pot full of dung. Animal droppings, for it is not customary to sow in such a pot.
and one may soak seeds in the Sabbatical year etc.. Because this soaking is not working the ground.

and one may keep aloe etc.. Aloe is a shrub with fleshy leaves, grown for ornament and medicine (aloe vera). The Kesef Mishneh explained that one may maintain it in the Sabbatical year, unlike other tender vegetables that grew on their own (below 4:18), because aloe usually grows by itself and no suspicion will arise that it was sown in the Sabbatical year, but watering it is forbidden because of this suspicion. Others explained that one may maintain it, meaning care for it in the permitted manner during the Sabbatical year, but not water it, since it can survive without watering, for its leaves are fleshy and store water (Rabbi Y. Felix on the Jerusalem Talmud, pp. 254-255).
one marks the tree with red dye. One marks it in red so that those who see it will pray for it not to shed its fruit (Babylonian Talmud Shabbat 67a).

and one loads it with stones. A tree that sheds its fruit because of excess richness and strength, one weakens its vigor by loading stones on it, thereby preventing the fruit from falling (Babylonian Talmud and Rashi there).
and they hoe. They hoe (this is also the reading in some versions).
and the one who loosens the soil. The hoer.
to improve. To enhance.
the cracks. The fissures in the wood.

if they were farther apart than ten to a beit se'ah. If the trees are planted at great distances, so that ten trees are spread over an area larger than a beit se'ah, which is an area suitable for sowing a se'ah of wheat (fifty cubits square, about 625 square meters).
they draw water from tree to tree. By means of channels.

the white soil. The portion of an orchard field that is suitable for sowing grain and legumes, where the trees are planted at great distances, according to the measure given at the start of the halakhah (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mo'ed Katan 2:10, and see also Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevi'it 2:1).
they sprinkle it with water. They drip a little water on it (but regular watering is forbidden, as stated at the start of the halakhah).
basins for vines. Hollows to collect water beneath the vines.
and they make the water channel at the outset. They dig a water channel.
the pools. Large hollows for collecting water, from which water is taken to water the trees.
as we explained. Above, halakhah 2.
plowed it. Turned over its soil.
and he may not sow it at the end of the Sabbatical year. In the entire year following the Sabbatical year.
and one may not lease it from him etc.. The Sages also forbade another person to sow it, if the field's owner receives a share of the crop.
and if he died, his son may sow it. For the son did not commit a prohibition, and there is no reason to penalize him (and compare below 3:11).
they did not penalize him. Since his actions in the Sabbatical year did not help prepare the ground for sowing, but only the plowing before sowing.
if some of the leaves were exposed, he need not worry. For that is the way of storing, not of sowing, and he does not want them to take root (Hilchot Kilayim 2:11).
the lof. A kind of onion.

it must not be less than four kavs, at a height of a handbreadth, with a handbreadth of earth over it. The Sages required that a large quantity of lof (four kavs) be buried together in a concentrated pile (a handbreadth high) and covered with a handbreadth of earth, for burying in this fashion does not look like sowing.
to stir. To mix with water the soil in which rice grows (which was sown in the sixth year), in order to maintain its moisture, because this is vital for the rice to survive.
but he may not trim. He may not trim the rice leaves.
a person may gather wood and stones etc.. If he needs the wood and stones.
the large ones. The large pieces of wood and stones.
so that he not say to him, "see what a favor etc.". For if he says this it is evident that he wants his fellow's field improved so that his fellow will return the favor.
for his animal testifies about him... his hired worker testifies about him. That he needs the grass or wood, and does not intend to improve the ground.
for wood. For the use of the wood.
it is permitted to uproot. To pull out the trees with their roots, even though his actions make the ground fit for sowing.
he cut down three... he may not uproot, for he is improving the land. For the size of the area of three trees is suitable for sowing (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevi'it 4:4).
from the ground. Close to the ground.
one who splits an olive tree. Cuts branches from it.
because it is work. For he improves the tree.
but he may cover with stones or straw. To prevent the tree from drying out.
one who trims the tails of vines. Cuts off their tails.
he may cut as is his way. If he needs the thing that is cut, and does not intend to improve the tree.
with an axe. A hatchet.
and with a saw. A kind of saw.
a virgin sycamore. A sycamore is a wild fig species; it is called virgin in its first growth, when it has never yet been cut.
not so that it will grow. Not in order to graft it anew.
but that it not split further. To split more.
that was cracked. That was split and cleft.
fertilizers. Organic waste that helps fertilize the ground, such as animal droppings or fruit peels.

and if he took out and set up a rubbish heap from it, it is permitted. If he designated a certain place for the manure where he piles it, he may take it out, since he does not look like one who is fertilizing, provided he observes the conditions later in the halakhah.

once it begins to form. Once it begins to ripen (and perhaps it means when its ripening is complete; see Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevi'it 3:1 in the various translations), and a sort of protrusions form on it.
the mattik. The bitter fruit of the colocynth plant, called "mattik" in euphemistic language (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.).
from one hundred fifty se'ah. About 1050 liters.
if he had a small amount. If he had a little manure in his field before the Sabbatical year (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevi'it 3:3).
he may keep adding to it. And he need not remove much at once.
and he may not make more than three rubbish heaps in each beit se'ah. For spreading manure in many places looks like fertilizing.
beit se'ah. See above 1:8.
three heaps of rubbish in each beit se'ah. Three piles of rubbish in each beit se'ah, and each pile has at least one hundred fifty se'ah of manure.
storehouse. One large pile with no limit on quantity.
or if he dug three handbreadths into the ground and set the manure in a heap. In such a way that the digging remains evident even after he placed the pile of manure in it (Yad Peshutah).
for the gathering of manure. For collecting the manure.
the sheep pen. A fenced place for gathering the flock.

in the way of all who gather manure. Under the conditions mentioned in the earlier halakhot, for the law of moving manure from the pen to the field is like the law of moving it from the courtyard to the field.

and one who makes a pen in his field in the Sabbatical year. In order to fertilize his field (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevi'it 3:4); they permitted this because he does not fertilize by hand, but the fertilizing happens by itself through the flock (Rabbi Y. Kafih and others). Some infer from the Rambam's wording here that the permission applies only when his intent is for the sake of the flock and not for fertilizing the field (Radbaz, Chazon Ish, Shevi'it 19:13, Rabbi Y. Kafih; and see Rabbi Avraham ben David).
beit sa'atayim. Fifty cubits by one hundred cubits (about 1200 square meters).
he leaves one wall of the pen's walls. He takes three walls out of the four walls of the pen, and leaves one wall in place.
and makes another pen beside it. By moving the three walls he removed to the other side of the wall that remained.
he leaves some of it. He leaves a small place in it unfertilized, as a reminder.
a person may not open a quarry etc.. He may not begin to quarry stones from a large rock in his field.
to improve his field. For sowing.
and split. Broke up, quarried.
twenty-seven stones in a square of three by three by a height of three. A square of three stones by three stones, which is nine stones, all of this multiplied by three layers.
each stone of them a cubit etc.. Large stones that are generally used for building.
at a height of a cubit. A cubit high.
it is permitted etc.. Provided that he does not intend to improve his field (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevi'it 3:5).
to quarry out. To hew out.
each one of them the load of two. Carried by two people together because of its weight.
for he takes it for the sake of the stones. For it is not customary to clear away a fence in order to sow in its place, and the stones themselves are also heavy and suitable for building.
it was less than ten. Handbreadths, so it is not considered a fence.

where he intended to improve his field. Where he takes the fence for the sake of using the stones as explained in the previous halakhah, and at the same time it is convenient for him that the place of the fence be improved for sowing after the Sabbatical year.
and he dismantles. He takes apart the fence (some versions read: "gorid" or "gomem," and see Rambam Meduyak by Rabbi Y. Shilat, that perhaps it should read "godeid").

even though he is a contractor. Who received the field to work for a share of the crop, nevertheless his law is that of a stranger with no interest in improving the field for sowing, since it is not known whether the field will be under his responsibility the next year as well.
stones that are fit etc.. That are not embedded deep in the ground.
two of the load of two each. Two heavy stones, each carried by two people, and which are therefore fit for building.
a heap of pebbles. A pile of small stones.
and if there is rock or straw beneath them etc.. Because everyone sees that he does not intend to sow.

a person may not fill a ravine etc.. A ravine is a slope that is customarily made fit for sowing by building retaining walls of stones (terraces) and filling the resulting space with earth. In the Sabbatical year it is forbidden to fill the area with earth, but the walls themselves, made of stones, may be built.

and any stone that he can... it may be taken. But a stone that he can take only by going down into the ravine, it is forbidden to take, since he looks like one improving his field for sowing (Commentary on the Mishnah and Rash, Shevi'it 3:8).
it is permitted to bring them from anywhere. Because they are used for building.
and likewise the contractor brings etc.. One who receives a field to work may bring stones from it; see above halakhah 8 for explanation.
a breach that is closed with earth. A stone fence between his field and the public domain that was breached, and in the place of the breach there is a mound of earth blocking it.
it is forbidden to build it. For he looks like one improving the field for sowing (Rivak"o and Radbaz).
or if it was not closed with earth... it is permitted to build it. For his intent is only to guard the field.

it is forbidden for him to build a fence in the Sabbatical year between his field and his neighbor's field. Since there is no great need for it, it appears that his intent is to prepare the field for sowing.
and it is permitted to deepen. In his digging for the sake of the fence.
in the way of all who pile manure. That is, he piles the earth as manure is piled in the Sabbatical year (above halakhot 1-3).
a pit, a trench, and a cave. Various forms of water reservoirs.
he piles the earth in his field in the way of all diggers. That is, they pile the earth in the manner of piling manure, so that he will not look like one improving the field.
a halakhah to Moshe from Sinai that it is forbidden. The mitzvah of this extension is not written explicitly in the Torah, but was transmitted by tradition.
when the Temple stands, it was forbidden by oral tradition. It is the tradition of the Sages that it was forbidden only in the time of the Temple.
Atzeret. The festival of Shavuot.
and the white field. A field designated for growing grain and legumes.
until Passover. For plowing after Passover no longer benefits the sixth-year grain, but prepares the ground for the Sabbatical year, and similarly for plowing an orchard field after Shavuot.
every three trees to a beit se'ah. In an area of a beit se'ah (see above 1:8) at least three trees are planted.
a barren tree. One that does not bear fruit.

they regard them as though they were figs, if they are fit to produce etc.. They estimate according to the size of the trees and the abundance of their branches how much fruit they would produce if they were fig trees.
if they are fit to produce. The three of them together (Rivak"o, and so it is implied in Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevi'it 1:4).
a cake of pressed figs. Pressed figs stuck together in the shape of a loaf of bread.
of sixty manah. Weighing sixty manah.

so that the cattle etc.. A yoke of oxen, which is a distance of four cubits (Babylonian Talmud Bava Batra 83a), for that is the way of planting trees, and if there is not that distance between them they will eventually be uprooted.

and one is fit to produce... and the two are not fit to produce a se'ah. It may mean that each one separately is not fit to produce a se'ah, which is about a third of the measure of sixty manah. For each of the trees must be fit to produce a third of sixty manah (according to the Ra'avad in his glosses and Shenot Eliyahu, Shevi'it 1:4). In most versions the word "se'ah" is missing, and according to this it may be sufficient that each tree be fit to produce any amount of the measure, provided the three together produce sixty manah (Rivak"o).

one plows for them only as much as they need etc.. Around the tree, in the place where the fig picker stands (the "orah") and where the fig basket is set beside it, one plows until Shavuot, and in the rest of the area until Passover.

even though some of them are not fit to produce. For if there are more than three trees, it is not necessary that each of them be fit to produce a part of sixty manah, but it suffices that three are fit.
until Rosh HaShanah. Of the Sabbatical year, since young saplings have not yet grown strong enough, and without this plowing they would spoil (Radbaz).
surrounded in a crown. Planted in a semicircle (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevi'it 1:6), and not scattered over the whole area.
but only as much as they need. Around the sapling to the full extent of the orah and its basket, and it is permitted to plow there until Rosh HaShanah (Derekh Emunah).
and it put forth replacements. It began to grow again.
and all these matters in the time of the Temple as we said. Above, halakhah 1.
the cucumber beds. A place where cucumbers are sown.
and the gourd beds. A place where gourds are sown.
and a beit hashelahin. A field needing constant irrigation (above 1:8).
and they fertilize, strip, dust, and smoke. Actions that benefit the tree (see in detail above 1:5 and the explanation there).
and they nibble, prune, and trim. Removing unwanted branches and parts of the tree.
and they apply foul odors to the saplings, bind them, and trim them. To protect the young trees (see above 1:5 and the explanation there).
and they make houses for them. Shelters to protect from rain or sun.
and they smear the unripe figs and pierce them. See above 1:5 and the explanation there.

unripe figs of the eve of the Sabbatical year that entered the Sabbatical year... one does not smear etc.. Fruits that did not finish ripening before the Sabbatical year may not be smeared or pierced in the Sabbatical year to hasten their ripening, because of the prohibition of work in the Sabbatical year.
and those of the Sabbatical year that went out into the end of the Sabbatical year, one does not smear etc.. Because the sanctity of the Sabbatical year applies to them.
on the slopes of the ravines. On the slopes of the mountains (see above 2:11 for this law in the Sabbatical year itself).
they graft... they layer. See above 1:4.
that the sapling take hold. That its roots spread in the ground.
two weeks. Two weeks, so that the permission to plant applies when at least forty-four days remain until Rosh HaShanah (until the fifteenth of Av).

lest an observer say, "they were planted in the Sabbatical year". For when one plants after this time, the years of orlah are counted from the following year (Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 9:8-10), and one who sees that the count of years begins from the Sabbatical year might think that planting in the Sabbatical year is permitted.
they require the heir to uproot. Because the concern "lest an observer say..." still exists (and compare above 1:13).
roots that were cut earlier and sprouted again. Plant roots that remained in the ground after the plant was cut, and grew again in the Sabbatical year.
sefiach. Appendages to the main crop.
that came up on their own and have no seed. For their way is to grow by themselves without human sowing.
that was well worked. That was plowed thoroughly.
and set up a heap. A large pile of grain.
and threshed with cattle. Separated the kernels from the ears by means of oxen dragging a threshing implement.
who reaped for the sake of working the land. So that the ground will produce better afterward.
as we explained. Above 1:1-2.
and beats. Separates the kernels by beating with a stick.
and by Rabbinic law. A decree of the Sages.
grain. The five species of grain (Hilchot Kilayim 1:8).
and legumes. Seeds that are human food, such as peas and rice (ibid.).
and garden seeds. Seeds of which one eats only the fruit without the seed, such as onion and other vegetables (ibid.).
fruits of trees. About which they did not worry regarding transgressors, since usually a tree that yields ripe fruit in the Sabbatical year was planted before the Sabbatical year.
the peigam. A wild plant with a sharp smell and yellow flowers.
and the yarbuzin. Kinds of asparagus.
the wild ones. That grow wild.
rabbinic lashes for rebelliousness. Lashes by Rabbinic law.
in an unplowed field. A field that was not plowed.
and in a plowed field. A field that was plowed but not sown.
a person does not turn his attention there. He does not invest his time in caring for it.
and a plowed field, he wants its improvement. To sow it at the proper time and in an orderly fashion.

and a vineyard field does not prohibit his vineyard. For one who sows grain or vegetables next to vines prohibits both for benefit because of kilayim of the vineyard (Hilchot Kilayim 5:7). And even though one who sows his vineyard in the Sabbatical year does not prohibit it (ibid. 5:8), people are nevertheless accustomed not to sow in a vineyard (Chazon Ish, Kilayim 3:29).
the straw. The waste of the grain, which is unfit for human food.
and they did not decree against it. For there is no concern that a person will sow for the sake of the straw.
that went out into the end of the Sabbatical year. That were not harvested until the eighth year.
are forbidden to eat. Lest he sow at the end of the Sabbatical year for the beginning of the eighth.

and one does not pull them up by hand, but plows as usual etc.. Some explained that it means that one may not pull them up by hand since their picking is forbidden (above halakhah 3), but one may plow and let the animal graze as usual, and there is no concern either about using sefiach as fertilizer for his field, or lest they sprout again (Yad Peshutah, Torat HaShemitah, pp. 561-562, see there; and see Chazon Ish, Shevi'it 9:6, who explained it otherwise).

and from Chanukah onward sefiach is permitted. Since produce sown in the eighth year is commonly found in the market, and there is no concern that a person will sow at the end of the Sabbatical year for this time. However, when it is known of a certain species that it is found in the market at an earlier time, it is permitted from that time, as explained in the next halakhah (Derekh Emunah, Yad Peshutah).
the grown ones are permitted. Since even the land that may be sown in the eighth year helps in their growth (see Hilchot Avodah Zarah 7:14).
onions that went out of the Sabbatical year into the end of the Sabbatical year. And were harvested in the eighth year.
if similar ones have been produced. If onions that were sown in the eighth year have already grown.
and so with the other fruits. Fruits of the ground.
one may buy. Purchase.
at the end of the Sabbatical year. In the eighth year.
if the early fruit ripened. If the first fruits of the eighth year ripened.
the late ones are permitted. It is permitted to eat of the Sabbatical year's fruits that remained and were late to ripen.

and it is permitted to buy vegetables immediately at the end of the Sabbatical year. Because vegetables grow very quickly (Pe'at HaShulchan 22:9). Some explain that it is because they were accustomed to bring vegetables from outside the Land (Radbaz; accordingly the permission applies only where vegetables from outside the Land are readily available; Orah V'Simchah based on the Chazon Ish).
luf. A kind of onion.
the new. Of the eighth year.

on the first of Tishrei, the New Year for Sabbatical years and Jubilees. The Sabbatical year and Jubilee begin then, and this is the determining date for the halachic status of the produce with regard to the laws of the Sabbatical year, as will be detailed in the following halachot (this date is also determinative for tithes; see Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 1:2-10).
and they reached the season of tithes. The stage of growth at which produce becomes obligated in terumah and tithes (see Hilchot Ma'aser 2:3-5).
with the sanctity of the Sabbatical year. As explained below in chapter 5.
and the Egyptian bean. A kind of legume found only in Egypt (Peirush HaMishnah, Nedarim 7:2).
that he sowed for seed. In order to take seeds from it, and not to eat the vegetable.
the completion of the fruit. Its full ripening (for the reason for the law, see the explanation in Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 1:8).
a vegetable at the time of its picking. The time of plucking the vegetable from the ground is the determining time for the laws of the Sabbatical year.

and the etrog etc.. Unlike other tree fruits, an etrog has the law of a vegetable, which follows the time of picking (Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 1:5). The reason is that the etrog requires abundant watering like vegetables (Bavli Kiddushin 3a).
like a bean. Small as a grain of a bean (a kind of legume), at the beginning of the etrog's ripening.
like a jar. Large as a jar, at the end of the etrog's ripening.

is obligated in tithes like the fruits of the sixth year. Fruits of the Sabbatical year are exempt from tithes (Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 6:5), and so an etrog picked in the Sabbatical year should be exempt from tithes, but with regard to this exemption the Sages were stringent and treated the etrog by the law of tree fruits, for which the determining time for tithes is when they begin to ripen.

it is like the fruits of the Sabbatical year and is tithed like the fruits of the sixth year, to be stringent. On one hand it has the sanctity of the Sabbatical year, and on the other hand they were stringent and obligated it in tithes (see also Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 1:6).

whether its vegetable... is permitted in the Sabbatical year. Even though it was picked in the Sabbatical year, since the vegetable is secondary to the seed and is judged as well by the time of full ripening (completion of the fruit).
and if he sowed it for a vegetable. For the purpose of eating it.
and the Sabbatical year came upon it. The Sabbatical year arrived before it was picked.
even its seed is forbidden. Since the seed is secondary to the vegetable and we follow the time of picking.

and likewise if he sowed it for seed and for vegetable, it is forbidden. The vegetable is forbidden because it is like sefichim (aftergrowth), and the seed is forbidden because of appearances (see Kesef Mishneh).

he transgressed and sowed it in the Sabbatical year and it came out in the eighth year. He sowed the Egyptian bean in violation in the Sabbatical year and its fruit ripened in the Sabbatical year, and it was picked in the eighth.

bnot shuach. A desert fig whose fruits are white (Peirush HaMishnah, Shevi'it 5:1). Some identify bnot shuach with the stone pine (a kind of pine), whose cone seeds are called pine nuts and are edible.
since they ripen after three years. Their ripening process takes three years.
if they reached the season of tithes. See above, halachah 9, for the explanation.
in the second year of the cycle. In the second year of the next Sabbatical cycle, which is the third year of their ripening process.
with the status of the Sabbatical year. With the sanctity of the Sabbatical year.

the sarisim onions. A kind of onion that requires abundant watering and is called 'saris' (barren) because, unlike other onions that sprout and put out leaves when placed in a damp place after being uprooted from the ground.
and the rain-fed (ba'al). Ordinary onions that get most of their life from rainwater.

from which he withheld three seasons. Three watering periods, and the fact that he withheld water from them shows that they reached the end of their ripening and are considered detached already from the sixth year (Peirush HaMishnah, Shevi'it 2:9).
the gourds that he kept for seed. That he left in the ground in order to produce seeds from them.
hardened. Dried out and became hard.
and became unfit for human food. They are not fit for human consumption.
it is permitted to keep them in the Sabbatical year. In order to sow from them after the Sabbatical year.
and likewise all vegetables that hardened before Rosh Hashanah, it is permitted to keep them in the Sabbatical year. For from the time they harden they are considered detached.

and if they were soft. At the beginning of the Sabbatical year, in which case they are treated like other vegetables that entered the Sabbatical year while still attached to the ground and are forbidden as sefichim.
it is forbidden to keep them because of sefichim. He must uproot them so that he not be suspected of having sown them in the Sabbatical year.

and we do not obligate him etc.. Luf (a kind of onion) and kanras (some identify it as artichoke) persist in the ground for a long time, and he will not be suspected of having sown them in the Sabbatical year (Torat HaKarka'ot, Shevi'it p. 507).
but he trims the leaves. He cuts off its tender leaves because of appearances.
luf of the eve of the Sabbatical year. Which needs only to be uprooted from the ground.
summer onions. That grow in the summer season, and are very dry onions.
and pu'ah. A plant from which a red dye is produced.
with axes. Hatchets.
and this is not working the land. For he does not intend to dig for sowing, but only to uproot.
onions etc.. This speaks of onions that ripened in the sixth year, and he left them in the ground so that they would dry, which have the law of onions that were uprooted (Yad Peshutah).
these are permitted. Since their growth is from the onion itself.

and if they turned black, they are like those planted in the ground. If their color turned dark green, this is a sign that they grew by drawing nourishment from the ground, and they are like Sabbatical year growths.
and its growths exceeded its original. The addition that grew in the eighth year is greater than the onion itself, which is forbidden as sefichim.
its growths raised its original. The onion is nullified by majority and its prohibition is lifted.
its nullification. Nullification of the Sabbatical year prohibitions.

he should not gather them as he gathers every year, as it says etc.. Surely the verse does not intend to forbid harvesting altogether, since it already says “and the Sabbath of the land shall be food for you” (Leviticus 25:6; and see above, halachah 1).
for the work of the tree. To improve it, for example by thinning out the poor fruit for the growth of the good fruit (see above 1:2).
they do not cut them in the designated place. They do not spread them out to dry in the place designated for that.
in a ruin. A desolate place.
in a trough. A vessel in which dough is kneaded, in which only a few grapes can be trodden.
and he may not make olives. He may not extract their oil.
but he crushes. He extracts the initial oil with a mortar.
and brings in a very small press. A very small press, unlike the usual way of pressing.

and he grinds in the olive press and brings in a small press. To extract more oil it is permitted to grind the olives in a mill, but afterward one may not put them in a large press as in other years, but in a small press.
to release. To declare ownerless.
fences. Encloses.
and everyone is equal. Everyone is permitted to take.
and he may bring etc.. The owner of the field may bring into his house.
and if he brought more than this it is permitted. They did not require him to remove what he brought in, even though he committed a prohibition.
whether or not in the presence of the Temple. Even when the Temple is not standing. And see further below 10:8-9 for when the Sabbatical year applies by Torah law.
all that those who came up from Babylonia took possession of etc.. The area of the Land of Israel that was under Israelite control during the Second Temple period, as detailed in Hilchot Terumot 1:8.
from Keziv to the river and to Amanah. In more detail there, halachah 7.
Syria. The lands conquered by David, as explained in Hilchot Terumot chapter 1, halachot 3-4, 9.
they decreed that it be forbidden to work. See also below 8:9.
for they are obligated in tithes by rabbinic law. By enactment of the prophets or the early Sages, as explained in Hilchot Terumot 1:1.
Transjordan. The eastern region that the tribes of Gad and Reuben and half the tribe of Manasseh inherited.
to the border. To the frontier.

and they plunder the Sabbatical produce. They would plunder and eat the produce outside of its sanctity (see below 5:13 that Sabbatical produce is not fed to a non-Jew), and would also cause the poor of Israel to remain without food (Aruch HaShulchan 16:8).

Sabbatical produce was given for eating, drinking, and anointing. As it says “and the Sabbath of the land shall be food for you” (Leviticus 25:6), and drinking is considered eating, and anointing, which is rubbing oil on the body, is considered drinking (Hilchot Terumot 11:1).
from tradition they learned 'shall be' etc.. The Sages received by tradition that this is to be learned from the word “shall be” (in the verse: “all its produce shall be for food”).
like the law of terumah and second tithe. See Hilchot Terumot 11:1-2, Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 3:11.
and he may not change fruits from their natural state. For example, by squeezing a fruit to extract a beverage from it (except for olives and grapes, which are permitted to be pressed; there).
animal food is not boiled. One does not boil animal food in water, since the way of animals is to eat food raw.
he does not busy himself etc.. He does not occupy himself with preparing it as human food (see also Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 3:11).

so that it not bring him to disqualification. So that he not cause a loss to the vegetable by making it forbidden to eat because of the oil mixed in it if the dish becomes impure (see below, halachah 17, that one may not cause loss to Sabbatical produce, and see Hilchot Terumot 3:1 that impure terumah is forbidden to eat).
for he did not leave it so as to come to disqualification. By eating immediately he reduced the concern that the dish would become impure.

he may not anoint with wine and vinegar. So the text in the printed editions. In the manuscripts the text is: “he may not anoint with wine and oil,” which is a scribal error (see Hilchot Terumot 11:1, Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 3:11).

and he may not perfume the oil. He may not add fragrant substances and the like that turn it into a medicinal ointment, because he thereby removes it from the category of food. But it is permitted to mix oil, wine, and spices for eating (Peirush HaMishnah, Terumot 11:1, Hilchot Terumot 11:3).
and he may not anoint in the bathhouse. Because of disrespect to Sabbatical produce.
one does not seal an oven or stove with it. One does not smear it over them to strengthen them or to close their cracks.

and one does not anoint with it with impure hands etc.. Because they make the oil impure, and people who are careful about purity cannot eat it. But if it fell on his flesh, it is permitted to make it impure, since it has already become repulsive and unfit for eating, and so the impurity does not reduce its use.
he rubs it. He rubs and anoints with it.
and he may not anoint his foot inside the shoe. Because part of the oil serves to anoint the shoe.

but he anoints his foot and puts on the shoe, and anoints his body etc.. In these cases the anointing of the body is done in the usual way, and therefore after anointing it is permitted for a person to make contact between his body and leather vessels, even though they are improved by the oil (see also Hilchot Terumot 11:6).
and rolls. Rolls around.
a katavliya. A leather mat used for lying on.
he sold it and bought other oil with it. He bought other oil with the money he received for the first oil.

both are forbidden for lighting, for one does not light with the proceeds of the Sabbatical year. For the proceeds of the Sabbatical year are permitted only for use for human food (see also below, halachah 12). And when he exchanged oil for oil, each of them is considered proceeds of the Sabbatical year, and therefore both are forbidden for lighting (and it seems that in the first case, where he sold it and bought other oil with it, only the oil he bought is forbidden for lighting).
and he may not put the oil into the fire. For this is not its way of use.
one dyes with them for a person. For a person's need.

for the sanctity of the Sabbatical year does not apply to dyes for animals. Plants used only for dyeing animals do not have Sabbatical sanctity, and we learn from this that dyeing for an animal is not an important use, and it is forbidden to do it with Sabbatical produce (Orah V'Simchah).
kinds of laundry agents such as borit and ahal. Plants that are not fit for eating but are used as laundry substances.
but one does not launder with Sabbatical produce. And laundering was permitted only with kinds intended for laundering, as detailed in the previous passage.
a melugma. A food that is chewed and placed on the skin for healing purposes.
for sprinkling. For example, sprinkling wine on the ground for a pleasant scent.
to vomit. To cause vomiting.
for soaking. Soaking in a Sabbatical beverage for softening and the like.
for laundering. Washing clothes.
a poultice. A bandage containing an ointment (Peirush HaMishnah, Eruvin 10:13).
and anything not designated for human food. But for animal food.
the siah, the hyssop, and the koranit. Wild plants from which spices can be produced.
it is like wood. Which does not have Sabbatical sanctity.
the stringencies of human food. The stricter laws that apply to human food.
for they are not boiled. As above, halachah 3.
it is permitted to sell etc.. See further below 6:1-3 for how it is permitted to sell Sabbatical produce.
to buy human food with them. To buy human food with the money he received.
but one does not sell animal food to buy other animal food with it. For one buys only human food with the proceeds of the Sabbatical year (see above, halachah 8, and below 6:1).

nor to a laborer. One may not give Sabbatical produce to a person hired to do work for him if it reduces his wages by the price of the produce, for one may not pay a debt with Sabbatical produce (see the next halachah, and see also below 6:11).
a weekly laborer. A laborer hired for a full week.
or whose food he fixed on top of his wages. Where he committed to provide him food without deducting it from his wages.
and one feeds the guests. Guests, since hospitality is considered an act of kindness and not repayment of a debt (Radbaz, and see the Piskei V'Shitot for another explanation).

and the court does not set for a woman etc.. A husband who left his home and left his wife without sustenance, the court allots her support money from his property (Hilchot Ishut 12:16), and they may not allot it to her from Sabbatical produce in her husband's fields.

but she is supported from her husband's. And although the husband is obligated to provide his wife's food, this is not considered repayment of a debt but like members of the household who are supported at his table.

but he may eat a little of them in the field when they are unripe, as he eats in the other years of the cycle. For it is people's way to eat a little of the fruit while unripe, casually (Peirush HaMishnah, Shevi'it 4:7).
until they reach the season of tithes. See above 4:9.
once they become glossy. Once they shine and become smooth.
and likewise all similar to them. In other fruits that typically become glossy, that he eats from them in the field from the time they are fit for casual eating.
and the unripe grapes (boser). Grapes that are not ripe.
once they emit water. So that they can be squeezed.
once a se'ah of olives yields a revi'it of oil. The olives grew enough that a revi'it of a log of oil can be pressed from a se'ah of olives.
he breaks. He breaks slightly.
they yielded half a log etc.. If half a log can be pressed from a se'ah of olives, they are fit for casual anointing.
he crushes. He mashes.

they yielded a third. If a third of a log can be pressed from a se'ah of olives, they are not fit for anointing at all, but are fit for regular eating in his home (Yad Peshutah based on Peirush HaMishnah).
it is permitted to cut down trees for wood. For the purpose of using the wood (but cutting in a destructive manner is forbidden in all years; see Hilchot Melachim 6:8-9).
for it has already put forth its fruit. Which are already fit for eating.
and the law of the Sabbatical year has lapsed from it. From the tree.
once they form chains. Once they form a kind of chain.
once they develop pits. Once they have pits in them.
once they sprout. Once they have buds, which are the beginning of the fruit.
once they put forth unripe fruit. Fruit that has begun to ripen.
the kafniyot. A cluster of dates at the beginning of its growth.
shitzin. Thorns.
straw. Grain waste.
and kash. Coarse straw.
in olive pomace. The waste of olives after the oil is extracted.
and in zuggin. Grape skins that have been pressed.

a bathhouse that was heated etc.. If they transgressed and burned Sabbatical straw and kash to heat a bathhouse, it is permitted to bathe there, since the prohibition has already been committed, and now the straw and kash are not fit for animal food.
for payment. Even for payment (and there is no concern about the prohibition of trading in Sabbatical produce mentioned below 6:1, because the straw and kash have already been burned).

lest they heat with it etc.. Straw and kash give off an unpleasant smell, and there is concern that the bath attendants will want to improve the smell for the honor of an important person (Radbaz in his second answer to the Raavad's critique, Aruch HaShulchan 24:31).

the peels and pits that are permitted in terumah to non-priests. Peels and pits that are not fit for eating, as detailed in Hilchot Terumot (11:10-11) regarding their permissibility to a person who is not a priest.
unless they are fit for dyeing. See further below 7:13-15.
and the kor. A white, soft piece of wood found at the top of the trunk of the date palm, which is fit for eating.
one who ties up spices etc.. One who places in a dish a tied bag with spices inside.
if their taste is nullified etc.. If the taste of the spices was absorbed in the dish and the spices themselves remain tasteless, it has the law of wood and has no Sabbatical sanctity.
it is like removed. Even though he committed a prohibition, we do not require him to remove the straw and kash from the cushion or the mortar, since they are considered nullified there.
it is cooled. He should cool it and not use the forbidden heat.
and once the second rainfall comes at the end of the Sabbatical year. In the second period of rainfall, at the beginning of the year after the Sabbatical year.
rainfall (revi'ah). A term for rains, so called because they make the earth fertile.
one may benefit and burn Sabbatical straw and kash. Because they have already rotted and are not fit for animal food (Yad Peshutah).
and that money etc.. The money he received for the produce became holy with Sabbatical sanctity, and food must be bought with it and eaten with Sabbatical sanctity.
and that fruit sold etc.. As detailed below, halachot 6-7.
field vegetables. Vegetables that grow on their own, which do not have the prohibition of sefichim (as mentioned above 4:3-4).
from Sabbatical peels. Peels that are fit for dyeing and have Sabbatical sanctity (above 5:21, below 7:15).
it is permitted to sell the surplus... and likewise if he gathered etc.. Since the vegetables came into his possession for his own use and not for the purpose of trade.
by measure. A volume measure.
by estimate (aksarah). By approximation and not precisely.
to make known that it is ownerless. That he acquired it from ownerless property for eating and not for the purpose of trade, and now wants to buy another food in its place.

and he bundles things that are usually bundled for the house. Vegetables that are liable to scatter are customarily tied in bundles, without being particular about a uniform quantity in each bundle, and this is how they bring them home.
not the way they bundle for the market. Not in bundles equal in quantity.
precisely. Exactly.

and things that are not usually bundled except for the market. For example, vegetables that do not tend to scatter, and there is no reason to bundle them unless one bundles them in equal bundles for commercial purposes.
they may not be sold etc.. Because he appears to be trading in Sabbatical produce.
and if they were recognizable. If everyone knows about them and recognizes them.
the Sabbatical year is more stringent than hekdesh. Sabbatical produce has a special stringency that does not exist for something consecrated to the Temple.
and the money takes hold in its place. The money became sanctified in place of the consecrated item.
they are not desanctified and made like the fruits of other years. They remained in their sanctity and did not become ordinary produce.

as it says of it 'it shall be' — 'in its being it shall be forever,' and since it is called holy it takes hold of its proceeds. On one hand we learn from the word 'shall be' that Sabbatical produce remains in its sanctity forever, and on the other hand we learn from the word 'holy' that money given in exchange for Sabbatical produce becomes holy with their sanctity, like the law of money given in exchange for consecrated items.
and he must remove both. To destroy the fruit and the meat.
at the time of removal of the Sabbatical produce. When the time arrives at which it is forbidden to eat the fruit (for the laws of removal see below chapter 7).
the meat went out and the fish were taken. The meat became ordinary again, and the fish became holy with Sabbatical sanctity.
and one does not make a melugma of either. It is forbidden to use them for healing, as mentioned above 5:10.
and one does not cause them loss. As mentioned above 5:17.

the Sabbatical year is desanctified only by way of purchase etc.. The sanctity of the Sabbatical year does not pass from the Sabbatical produce ('first fruit') to another item except through sale of the produce.

but with second fruit etc.. Something received in exchange for Sabbatical produce and made holy with its sanctity can return to being ordinary even without transferring ownership, by applying the sanctity to money or a food item.
fruit purchased a second time. Second fruit.

lest he leave them and raise flocks upon flocks from them. Lest the animal made holy with Sabbatical sanctity give birth to holy offspring, and he will not be careful about their sanctity as he should.
and needless to say the Sabbatical produce itself. When he desanctifies it by way of purchase, one may not buy a live animal in exchange for it.
those fruits. That were bought in exchange for Sabbatical produce or the proceeds of the Sabbatical year.
on the slaughtered ones. Which have the law of food.
proceeds of the Sabbatical year etc.. And similarly with the poor tithe (Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 6:17) and the second tithe (Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 3:21).
one does not repay a debt with them. Because of the prohibition of trading.

and one does not make a shoshvinut with it. A sum of money that was given to a groom to help with his wedding needs (the details of the matter are explained in Hilchot Zechiyah U'Matanah chapter 7). It is forbidden to give this sum from the proceeds of the Sabbatical year, because if the recipient does not return it to the giver when the giver marries, he can sue him in court, and so giving a shoshvinut is considered a loan or a commodity (Torat HaKarka'ot, Pe'ah p. 189, Orah V'Simchah).
and one does not pay recompense with them. A person who received a favor from his fellow may not give Sabbatical proceeds in return, as this is considered repayment of a debt.
and one does not pledge charity to the poor in the synagogue with them. A person who committed to donate a certain sum may not pay his obligation with Sabbatical proceeds.
but one may send with them acts of kindness. In a way that he does a favor for his fellow that he is not obligated to do.
and he must inform. So that the recipient knows that he must treat them with Sabbatical sanctity.
and an unclean animal. Which is not fit for eating.

and if he bought, he eats an equivalent. If he mistakenly bought with Sabbatical proceeds something unfit for eating, he should buy with ordinary money ordinary produce in the same amount as the sum he erred with, and eat it with Sabbatical sanctity.
as he does with second tithe. See Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 7:17.
the nests of zavim, zavot, and women after childbirth. A pair of birds that the zav, the zavah, and the woman after childbirth bring as offerings (see Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:3).
to the bath attendant. The owner of a bathhouse.
to the boatman. The owner of a ship.
but he may give etc.. It is permitted to give Sabbatical proceeds to a person who draws water with a bucket, since the payment is for water for drinking.
an issar. A silver coin.
his wages are permitted. The money is ordinary, since it was given to the laborer as wages for his work and not as payment for Sabbatical vegetables.
and they did not penalize etc.. Will be explained in the next halachah.
and if he said, 'Gather vegetables for me with it today'. This wording implies that the money was given as payment for the vegetables, and therefore it becomes Sabbatical proceeds.
the donkey drivers. Riders of donkeys.
more than enough. See above 4:24.
and this is a penalty for them. Although they received payment for their work (and not as payment for the produce), the Sages penalized them for bringing too much.
because the laborer's wages etc.. The Sages did not penalize a laborer who gathered too many vegetables, since his wages are limited and essential for his survival.
the baker. A baker.
a loaf. Bread.
for a pundyon. A sum of money.
I will bring you with it. I will give you in exchange for the loaf.
this is permitted. For it is permitted to exchange Sabbatical produce for other food.
and if he took from him without specifying. Without saying how he will pay him.
they eat Sabbatical produce with favor. In a way that he feels indebted to the one who gave him the produce.
he eats them etc.. He may eat these fruits alone, even though he feels indebted to the giver or the one who bequeathed (Peirush HaMishnah, Shevi'it 9:9).

and for your animal and for the beast etc.. This verse was said following the verse “and the Sabbath of the land shall be food for you...,” and from the proximity of the verses it implies that it is permitted to eat Sabbatical produce on condition that it is still available for the beasts in the field.
ended. Finished.
to remove. To destroy.
dried figs. Dried figs.
for the figs are on the trees in the field. For there are moist, fresh figs on the trees.
he had a lot of fruit. And the time of removal approaches.
he distributes them as food etc.. So that they eat them that day, and he will not need to destroy the fruit.
those who eat. People who will eat.
because they are not found for the beast. Wild animals eat only in places that are not guarded.
but if there is there etc.. If there are grapes in the field that take a long time to ripen, it is permitted to eat the raisins in the house.
twice a year. In two seasons of blossoming.
autumn fruits. Fruits that ripen in the autumn season of the eighth year.
because they resemble the fruits of another year. Even though they began to grow in the Sabbatical year.

one who pickles three pickles etc.. One who pickles three kinds of pickled vegetables in one barrel, and opens the barrel after the time of removal has arrived for some of the kinds, need not remove a kind whose time of removal has not arrived, even though it absorbed taste from a kind that requires removal.

and if he began it, everything is as removed. If he opened the seal of the barrel before the time of removal arrived, he may eat its contents as long as he wishes even though the time of removal has arrived, because pickles spoil if not eaten within a short time, and therefore they are considered removed (Aruch HaShulchan 27:24, Orah V'Simchah, R. Y. Kafah; and see Peirush HaMishnah, Ma'aser Sheni 5:6).
the money. Money received in exchange for Sabbatical produce.
and he eats with their proceeds. He buys foods in order to eat them with Sabbatical sanctity.
to the Dead Sea. The sea whose waters are salty and cause coins to be consumed (the Dead Sea is the Great Sea; Hilchot Arachin V'Charamin 8:8 according to accurate versions).
three lands for removal. The Land of Israel is divided into three regions for the time of removal.
Transjordan. The eastern region.
to the sea. The Kinneret.
until the last of it is finished. Until the fruit is finished in all the fields in the region, since the animals go looking for food throughout the region.
until the last in Zoar is finished. Until the dates are finished in the city of Zoar near the Dead Sea.
until Purim. In the eighth year (and so too for the other times mentioned here).
Atzeret. The festival of Shavuot.

and for grapes... and for dried figs etc.. For these fruits as well the Sages set a uniform date for all parts of the Land, for the sake of the common people who do not know the exact time of removal (Yad Peshutah).
because the stringencies of the place are imposed on it etc.. See also Hilchot Yom Tov 8:20.
and the produce of the Land that went out outside the Land. In violation, since it is forbidden to take Sabbatical produce outside the Land (above 5:13).
is removed in its place. And he need not return it to the Land of Israel.
and he may not transfer them from place to place. Rather he removes them in the place where they are when the time of removal arrives.
from the dyeing kinds. Plants from which dye is produced.
if it does not persist in the ground. It does not remain from year to year.
it has Sabbatical status and its proceeds have Sabbatical status. The laws of the Sabbatical year apply to it, and also to money received in exchange for it if it was sold.
the luf. A kind of onion.
the dandanah. Mint.
and the ulshin. Some identify it with cultivated chicory, and some identify it with garden bitter herb.
thorns and thistles. Kinds of thorns.
isatis. A plant from which a blue dye is produced.
and kotzah. A plant called safflower, from which an orange dye is produced.
the pu'ah. A plant from which a red dye is produced.

and the rikhpah. A tree from which a red dye is produced (according to the Rambam's identification in Peirush HaMishnah, Shevi'it 7:2; some explain that it is a plant from which a yellow dye is produced).

rather one benefits and dyes with it until Rosh Hashanah. And all the more so after the Sabbatical year (Rikevo and Kesef Mishneh, and in accordance with the Raavad's view in his critique that it is permitted to benefit from it forever, and the Chazon Ish, Shevi'it 13:9, wrote that the Rambam should read “after Rosh Hashanah”). Some explain the Rambam's words to mean that initially it is proper to use it in the Sabbatical year and not to keep it for the eighth year, lest he forget to treat it with sanctity (Yad Peshutah).

and anything not designated etc.. This halachah speaks of plants that have Sabbatical sanctity because they are somewhat fit for animal food, but are not obligated in removal, because they are not an ordinary food of animals (Aruch HaShulchan 28:5, Chazon Ish, Shevi'it 13:9, and similarly in Yad Peshutah).
since it is not for wood. It is not used for fuel and the like (and wood has no Sabbatical sanctity; above 5:11).
root. Root.
and the akravanin. A perennial plant identified in our day as a species of fern called the beautiful maidenhair (according to Peirush HaMishnah, Shevi'it 7:2).
pomegranate peels. The rinds of the pomegranate.
and its nitz. The protruding nub inside the crown of the pomegranate (Peirush HaMishnah, Shevi'it 7:3, Uktzin 2:3).
and the pits. The pits of all fruits.
they have Sabbatical status. If they are fit for animal food or for dyeing.
but neither they nor their proceeds require removal. Since they are not designated for these uses (Yad Peshutah, and as above, halachah 14).
the tender shoots of zeradin and carobs. The tips of the tender branches at the time of the trees' blossoming, which are fit for eating by pickling (Peirush HaMishnah, Shevi'it 7:5).
the elah. The oak tree (there).
and the batnah. Another species of the elah tree, whose fruit is called pistachio (there).
and the atadim. A kind of thorn that yields hard black berries that are fit for eating (there).

they and their proceeds have Sabbatical status, and neither they nor their proceeds require removal. The tender branch tips ('shoots') of all of these are fit for eating, but they have no obligation of removal because they do not decay but harden on the tree (Chazon Ish, Shevi'it 14:1).
but their leaves require removal. Because they fall off.
what is the time of removal of the leaves. When must the leaves that were kept for eating be removed from the house.
until they wither. Until they fall off.
the matik. The bitter fruit of the colocynth plant, called 'matik' (sweet) euphemistically (Peirush HaMishnah, Shevi'it 3:1).
and he gathers. He collects.
the second rainfall at the end of the Sabbatical year. The second rainy period in the eighth year.
until the second rainfall comes. For until then there is ownerless Sabbatical fruit in the orchards (Peirush HaMishnah, Shevi'it 9:7).
and the kofer. A shrub called henna (according to the first explanation in Peirush HaMishnah, Shevi'it 7:6), from whose flowers perfume is produced.

and the lotem. A tree whose fruits are today's chestnuts or a kind of pine tree (both explanations in Peirush HaMishnah there; some explain that it refers to the plant still called lotem today, some species of which are used to produce cosmetics and perfumes).
sap that comes from trees and from roots. Fragrant substance that comes from trees and roots.
the unripe fruit (paggin). Fruit that has not ripened.
like their fruit. Since a non-fruit-bearing tree does not make fruit, the sap that comes from it is considered like fruit (Orah V'Simchah and Yad Peshutah).

and the oil is permitted. Since a new rose does not give flavor to old oil (which remained from the sixth year) except through prolonged steeping, and therefore it has no Sabbatical sanctity (Peirush HaMishnah, Shevi'it 7:7).

he pickled it in oil from the end of the Sabbatical year etc.. In the reverse case, where the rose is old (left from the Sabbatical year) and the oil is new, the oil immediately absorbs the taste of the rose and becomes obligated in removal (there).
carobs of the Sabbatical year etc.. Since either way they give taste to wine after brief steeping (there).

a kind with its own kind in any amount. A Sabbatical food that was mixed with food of the same kind, even if the Sabbatical produce was in a small amount (for example, one drop of Sabbatical wine mixed into a barrel of sixth-year wine), makes the entire mixture obligated in removal (see also Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 15:8).
and not of its own kind, by giving taste. Sabbatical food or drink mixed with a different kind does not cause it to become obligated in removal, unless it gave taste in it.
to strengthen. To encourage or assist.

for it is forbidden to strengthen the hands of transgressors. So they learned from the verse “and before the blind you shall not place a stumbling block” (Leviticus 19:14), that it is forbidden to cause additional stumbling to a person who does not see the path of truth (Peirush HaMishnah, Shevi'it 5:6).
to one who is suspected regarding the Sabbatical year. Who is known not to be careful about the laws of the Sabbatical year.
the yoke. The implement placed on an animal by which it pulls the plow.
and the winnowing fork. An implement for winnowing grain (similar to a pitchfork).
and the digger. A digging tool.
anything whose function is designated for work that is forbidden in the Sabbatical year. An implement designed for forbidden work, with no other use.
and for work that could be forbidden and could be permitted. An implement used for work that can also be done permissibly.
the sickle. A harvesting tool.
for if he reaps... and if he reaps etc.. Since it is possible to reap in the permitted manner (as explained above 1:4), the seller need not worry that the buyer will reap in the forbidden manner.

and it is permitted to sell without specification etc.. Even if the buyer did not explicitly say what the purpose of the purchase is, since he is not suspected, we assume that he intends a permitted use at the end of the Sabbatical year.
the potter. A craftsman who makes clay vessels.
five jars of oil and fifteen jars of wine. Empty jars, since the buyer is permitted to bring into his house oil and wine in such a quantity (as mentioned above 4:24).
to let it lie fallow. To leave it fallow, without plowing and sowing.
but he may not sell him a tree field. Because it is almost certain that one suspected of this will not treat the fruit by the laws of the Sabbatical year (Aruch HaShulchan 29:4).
unless he stipulates with him that he has no part in the tree. He sells him the field without the tree.
se'ah. A measuring vessel (named for the volume measure it holds).
threshing floor. A place for beating harvested grain.
and all of them are explicitly forbidden. If he said explicitly that he wants to use them for a forbidden purpose, it is forbidden to assist him.
a sifter. A utensil for sifting flour.
and a sieve. A utensil for sifting seeds.
a mill. A grinding implement.
you shall sort. You shall select.

and it is permitted to pick fruit with them. To pick fruit from a detached branch (Yad Peshutah). Perhaps it refers to any picking, so that in plowing and sowing it is forbidden to assist but in picking it is permitted (R. Y. Shilat in his notes to the corrected Rambam).
and leases. Rents in exchange for a share of the crop.
plowed fields. Fields that were plowed, and this speaks of a non-Jew's field that he plowed in the Sabbatical year, and a Jew wants to sow in it after the Sabbatical year.
because they are not obligated, so as to penalize them. Unlike a Jew's field that he plowed in the Sabbatical year, which is forbidden to sow, as mentioned above 1:13.

it is permitted to do work on detached produce in Syria etc.. Although the Sages forbade working the land in Syria (above 4:27), it is permitted to assist non-Jews there with work done after the produce has been detached.
threshing. Beating the grain.
and winnowing. Scattering the grain in the wind to remove the waste from it.
and treading. Grapes in the winepress.
and gathering sheaves. Gathering the grain into piles.
and they do not harvest grapes. They do not pick grapes.
and they do not pick olives. They do not harvest olives.
to buy. To purchase.
lest he not eat them with Sabbatical sanctity. For the money received for the produce becomes holy with its sanctity, and food must be bought with it and eaten with sanctity (as mentioned above 6:1).

one who buys a lulav etc.. One who buys the four species from an am ha'aretz should ask him for the etrog as a gift, since an etrog picked in the Sabbatical year has Sabbatical sanctity (see above 4:12), and if he pays for it, he is handing Sabbatical proceeds to an am ha'aretz.
and if he did not give it to him etc.. If the seller did not agree to give him the etrog as a gift, he pays him a high price for the lulav that also includes the price of the etrog.
when does this apply. That it is forbidden to buy Sabbatical produce from an am ha'aretz in any amount.

fruits like them are guarded. Valuable fruits that are customarily guarded, and in a Sabbatical year they must be declared ownerless (and because there is reasonable concern that he committed a prohibition and did not declare them ownerless, they did not make it lenient for him in the manner explained later in the halachah).
the pegam. A wild plant with a pungent smell and yellow flowers.
and the yarbuzin. Kinds of asparagus.
the wild (shotin). Those that grow wild.
and the chalogelogot. A wild plant that grows from irrigation in the summer months, called purslane.
and the coriander of the mountains. Coriander that is not cultivated but grows wild in the mountains.

to buy from him a little, for the price of only three meals. To buy from him a small sum appropriate for buying three meals, but no more, since the money handed to the seller becomes holy with Sabbatical sanctity.

because of the livelihood of the seller. They were lenient in handing an am ha'aretz a small sum of Sabbatical proceeds for his essential sustenance ('bare life'), on the assumption that he will not trade with such a sum and will not keep it until the time of removal but will buy foods with it.

and likewise something not obligated in tithes... and Egyptian lentils. For it is not customary to sow them and their presumption is that they come from ownerless property (Peirush HaMishnah, Ma'aserot 5:8, Hilchot Terumot 2:12).

weeping garlic and the onion of Rikhpah. Garlic and onions that are very pungent and cause tears to flow (Peirush HaMishnah there; some explain that they are named for their place; see the commentators on the Mishnah there).
and Cilician groats. Grains of beans that grow in Cilicia (there).

one may not buy from him anything that has a shade of Sabbatical year at all, and one may not buy from him etc.. It is forbidden to buy from him anything connected to Sabbatical sanctity, such as flax, for flax seed has Sabbatical sanctity, and it is forbidden to buy from him even the flax itself, which has no sanctity, unless a significant change has been made in it, such as the flax fibers being made into spun threads from which a garment can be made or woven into braided ribbons like chains (Orah V'Simchah and Yad Peshutah based on Peirush HaMishnah, Bekhorot 4:8).
one suspected regarding tithes. Who sells second tithe without informing the buyer of its sanctity.

tithe requires bringing to the place. Second tithe has a special stringency, that it must be brought up to Jerusalem and eaten there (Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 2:1), and it is possible that one who trades in Sabbatical produce takes care not to cause stumbling with second tithe produce.
and the Sabbatical year has no redemption. Sabbatical produce has a special stringency, that it cannot be made ordinary (as above 6:6).
who sold it with the presumption of being pure. So that the buyer thinks it is pure.

he does not make others impure except by rabbinic law. As explained in Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot chapter 7, and so the seller is not suspected of causing stumbling in a Torah prohibition (see also Hilchot Metam'ei Mishkav U'Moshav 10:11).
he is trusted regarding that of others. He is trusted to say about another person's merchandise that it is kosher.
the presumption is that a person does not sin for others. We assume that a person will not lie and cause people to stumble for the benefit of another person (see also Hilchot Ma'aser 12:17).
he judges him and testifies about him. He is permitted to judge others or to testify about them, although he himself sins in the matter being judged (Hilchot Metam'ei Mishkav U'Moshav 10:11).

since terumot are permitted to us etc.. The prohibition of eating terumah for one who is not a priest ('a stranger') is a severe prohibition punishable by death at the hands of Heaven (Hilchot Terumot 6:6), unlike Sabbatical produce, which does have certain restrictions but carries no death penalty. From this the priests mistakenly conclude that if they are permitted to eat terumah, all the more so they need not be careful about the laws of the Sabbatical year.

a se'ah of terumah that fell into a hundred se'ah of Sabbatical produce is lifted out. When terumah is mixed with ordinary produce that outnumbers it a hundredfold, the law is that an amount equal to the terumah that was mixed in is removed from the mixture and given to the priests, and the rest is permitted to eat (see Hilchot Terumot 13:1).

if it fell into less than a hundred etc.. When there are not a hundred parts of ordinary produce against the terumah, the whole becomes 'mixed with terumah,' which is forbidden for an Israelite to eat and must be sold to priests (there 13:2). But with Sabbatical produce this cannot be done, and one must wait until all the fruit rots and throw it away.
and the fatteners. Those who fatten animals.
they buy. They purchase.
bran. The waste of flour.
from anywhere. Even from an am ha'aretz, but not from one who is suspected (Rikevo based on the Yerushalmi, and as above, halachah 14).
charity collectors. Those appointed to distribute food to the poor (see Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 9:1-3).
they need not be particular with the courtyards of those who eat Sabbatical produce. They need not be concerned about receiving Sabbatical produce for the poor.
Sabbatical coins or eggs bought with Sabbatical proceeds. For the common people do not know that the money becomes holy with Sabbatical sanctity (Radbaz).

let every creditor release what he lent. The 'ba'al masheh yado' is the creditor who claims his money (see Onkelos), and he must release in the Sabbatical year the loan “that he lent to his neighbor.”
when the Jubilee applies. When all of Israel is on its land (below 10:8).
for there is a release of land there. Purchased lands return to their original owners.
tradition. A received tradition.
and there it says. In the mitzvah of Hakhel.
just as there it is after seven. At Sukkot of the eighth year.
so too the release of monies is after seven. At the end of the Sabbatical year.
and divided it with the intention that today is the New Year at the end of the Sabbatical year. And they will pay him for the meat after the festival.

and Elul was intercalated. The court determined that the month of Elul would be extended (a month of thirty days), and Tishrei would begin only the next day. This situation applies at a time when there is a Sanhedrin, and the calendar is not known in advance but is set by sighting the moon (see Hilchot Kiddush HaChodesh 1:3-4, 5:1).
the money was lost. He lost his money.
a loan with a document that has liability of properties. In the loan document it is written that the borrower's lands are pledged for repayment of the debt.
and if he designated a field for him for his loan. They agreed between them on a particular plot of land from which the lender could collect his debt.
he does not release. Since such a debt is considered one that has already been repaid (similar to the loan on a pledge mentioned below, halachah 14).
releases the oath. A person who owed his fellow a monetary oath need not swear.
with the oath of the judges. An oath that the court administers to the defendant regarding his claim (see Hilchot Shevuot 11:4-6).

of matters that if he admits them, the Sabbatical year releases. The monetary dispute is about a debt, so just as the Sabbatical year releases the debt itself, it releases an oath obligation that stems from a dispute about the debt.

but the oath of guardians... where if he admits, he pays. In the case where the oath of the judges is connected to a monetary dispute that does not stem from a debt but from a deposit, partnership, and the like, which the Sabbatical year does not release, the oath is not released.
and he claimed it from him and he denied it. The lender asked for his money, and the borrower denied it.

the Sabbatical year does not release. Since at the time of release we do not know whether there was a loan or not, as the borrower denies it, and for example where the borrower has not yet been obligated to swear (Radbaz, and see another explanation in Yad Peshutah).
and he set a time for him of ten years. So that he cannot claim it until ten years pass (Hilchot Malveh V'Loveh 13:5). And the same is true if he set another time that ends after the Sabbatical year.
for he comes to 'he shall not press'. After ten years.
he is now. At the time of the release.

he stipulated with him that he will not claim it, the Sabbatical year releases. In this case the obligation to repay applies to the borrower all along, although the lender cannot claim it, and so this loan is like any loan (Rikevo and others).
for he cannot cancel the law of the Sabbatical year. Such a condition has no meaning, since he stipulated to cancel a Torah law (see Hilchot Ishut 6:9-10).
shop credit. A regular customer in a shop who from time to time pays all at once for the purchases he made recently.
is not released. It is not yet considered a debt, since the seller does not want to collect the payment until a significant sum accumulates (see Peirush HaMishnah, Shevi'it 10:1).
and if he made it a loan. From the moment the seller wants to collect the payment (and see further in the Piskei V'Shitot).
a laborer's wages are not released. Since it is the way of workers to wait before demanding wages until a significant sum accumulates (Kesef Mishneh).
and if he converted it into a loan. If he made it a debt.
and if he converted them into a loan. If he made them a debt on the penalized party, for example by writing a promissory note for payment of the fine (see below, halachah 13 for the explanation).

and from when are they converted into a loan: from the time of standing trial. From the time they stood him in judgment, it is possible to convert it into a loan, because from that time the fine's belonging to its recipient is established (Yad Peshutah, and see also Hilchot Na'arah Betulah 2:15).
fines of the rapist, the seducer, and the one who spreads a bad name. Fixed sums that the Torah obligated one who commits these acts to pay (see Hilchot Na'arah Betulah 1:1, 3:1).
are not released. Since they are not like an ordinary monetary debt toward another person, but a punishment (Peirush HaMishnah, Shevi'it 10:2).

her ketubah is not released. Since a ketubah document has the force of a judgment written by a court ('an act of the court' — Rashi, Gittin 18a), and such a debt is not released, as below, halachah 15.
she impaired it. She admits she received part of the sum (Hilchot Ishut 16:14).
she converted it into a loan against him. By writing a promissory note (Responsa of the Rambam, nos. 201 and 233).
one who lends against a pledge. A lender who took a security from the borrower.
does not release. Since the pledge is acquired by the lender (temporarily), and this is like a debt already repaid (Peirush HaMishnah, Shevi'it 10:2).
provided that the debt corresponds to the pledge. That the pledge's value equals the amount of the debt.
and if it was more. If the amount of the debt is greater than the value of the pledge.
he releases the excess over the pledge. The difference between the amount of the debt and the value of the pledge is released.
that they decided. That they ruled.
beware etc.. From this we learn that one should not refrain from lending before the Sabbatical year out of concern that the debt will be released.

he instituted the prozbul so that the debt not be released. The word prozbul comes from Greek, and its exact meaning is not entirely clear. The prozbul is a declaration by the lender before a court that he will collect his debts at any time (below, halachah 18). Hillel the Elder instituted that at a time when the release of monies applies by rabbinic law, if a person declares to the court that he will collect his debts whenever he wishes, it is considered as if he had handed over the documents to the court (Rikevo, above, halachah 15).
with the release of monies in our time etc.. As above, halachot 2-3.
a court of the greatest sages etc.. Who have great authority in public matters.
the text of the prozbul itself. The wording of the prozbul.
I hand over to you. I declare before you (Peirush HaMishnah, Shevi'it 10:4).
that any debt I have. Any debt owed to me.

a prozbul is written only on land. Unless the borrower has land. Some explain the reason is that then the debt is considered collected in the court's hands, similar to the law of a loan on a pledge above, halachah 14 (Rash, Shevi'it 10:6).
he had. The borrower.
a mortgaged field. A field that he gave as security for another loan, even if the field is currently in the possession of the lender and he eats its produce (Peirush HaMishnah, Shevi'it 10:6).
and for orphans. Who borrowed money and have no land.

guardians (apitropin). Those responsible for the orphans. [Note: the vocalization of the word follows the Greek origin. In the Rambam's own handwritten Peirush HaMishnah several forms of vocalizing this word appear: sometimes the first pe is vocalized with a kubutz, sometimes with a patach (and in some places the pe is not vocalized).]
and for a guarantor. A person who committed to pay the debt if the borrower does not pay.
if he had a debt from his fellow. If another person owes the borrower money.
since it is under his lien. Since this land is pledged to the borrower.
to each and every one. Since there are five lenders, and the prozbul is written by the lender and not by the borrower.
it is not effective. For a prozbul cannot be written on a debt that does not yet exist.
it is not released by this prozbul. The prozbul is effective so that the loan is not released.
it is released. Unless he writes another prozbul after the loan.
an antedated prozbul. A prozbul written on a certain date, in which they wrote an earlier date.
and he antedated its date from Adar. The date written in the prozbul is the month of Adar.
for his power was weakened. The power of the lender who wrote the prozbul.
for it does not release only until Adar. The lender relies on this prozbul only for loans he made up to Adar.
but if he postdated and wrote it from Iyar. If the prozbul was written in Nisan, and the date written in it is the month of Iyar.
for he does not release etc.. The error in the date causes the lender not to release loans he made up to Iyar, although the prozbul is effective only for loans up to Nisan.
the danger. A decree by non-Jews against observance of mitzvot, because of which they were afraid to keep prozbuls (Kesef Mishneh).

and onward. And even after the danger had passed, the Sages decided to leave in place the law that was newly established at the time of the danger. This decision is also based on the reason explained below, halachah 26 (see Orah V'Simchah, Yad Peshutah).
and the orphans. Who inherited a promissory note from their father (Responsa of the Rambam, no. 290).

do not need a prozbul. For if they are minors, the court claims their debts, and their documents are considered handed over to the court even without a prozbul. And if they are adults, the court argues on their behalf that their father had a prozbul. However, in a case where the father said before his death that he had no prozbul, adult orphans cannot collect the debt (there).

for if he said etc..
